# dsh-installed-plugins
**A plugin catalog for DeepSeek Harness — stop wondering what all those plugins you installed actual
in catalog for DeepSeek Harness — stop wondering what all those plugins you installed actually do.**
Installs a **Plugin Catalog** tab into the DSH settings page. It lists every third-party plugin in y
our profile with a plain-language description of what it does, its installed version, whether it is
actually assembled, and whether a newer version exists on npm.
> 中文说明见文末 · Jump to Chinese
## What you get
| 🗂 **One list, everything explained** | Every third-party plugin in your profile, with what it does

and how to use it. |
| 🔄 **Rebuilds itself** | The host watches your profile's `package.json`. Inst

all or remove a plugin and the catalog updates on its own — no command to run, no page reload. |
| 🆕
**New-plugin marker** | Anything that appeared since the last snapshot is badged and highlighted, s

o a fresh install never slips by unnoticed. |
| ⬆️ **Update check** | One click queries the npm regi

stry and shows `1.7.25 → 1.7.29` plus an *update available* badge. |
| 🛡 **Compatibility verdict** |
Before anything is installed, each update is checked for real breakage: a raised peer requirement,
a reverse constraint from another installed plugin, a Node engine mismatch. Verdicts are *safe* / *h

as risk* / **incompatible** — an incompatible one requires an explicit force. |
| 🚀 **Update one, or
all** | Tick what you want and hit *update selected*, or use *update all*. Incompatible entries are

never swept up silently. |
| 📜 **Changelog in place** | Every pending update can show its release n

otes, pulled from GitHub Releases or from the changelog file shipped in the package. |
| ↩️ **Backup
+ rollback** | `package.json` and the lockfile are copied to `backup-update-<timestamp>/` before an

ything changes, and restored automatically if the install fails. |
| 🗄 **WebDAV backup & restore** |
Push the whole plugin setup — dependency specs, load order, local `.mjs` plugins, both patch layers
, embedded local tarballs — to a WebDAV share as one JSON file, and rebuild it on another machine fr

om the panel. |
| 🗑 **Uninstall from the panel** | Remove a plugin *and everything that assembles it
*: the dependency, its `dsh.profile.bundles` entry, and any `cordis.patch.yml` row that loads it. Yo

u see the plan first. |
| 📄 **`PLUGINS.md`** | The same data as a greppable, git-friendly Markdown f

ile. Write it on demand from the panel. |
| 🔍 **Search & filter** | Instant client-side search over

names, descriptions and tags. Zero round trips. |

## Where descriptions come from
Three layers, highest priority first. You only ever have to write the top one.
| Layer | File | Who writes it |

| **Your notes** | `data/plugins.json` | You. Never overwritten, and gitignored — it is yours. |
| *
*Shipped descriptions** | `data/known-plugins.json` | This package. Covers ~20 popular community plu

gins so a fresh install is useful immediately. |
| **npm fallback** | the installed package's own `d
escription` | Nobody — read straight off the package. |

WebDAV credentials are **not** configured here — they live in the panel (and its `settings.json`), s
o they can be changed without editing this file or restarting DSH.
**`dataDir` defaults** — a `link:`/checkout install keeps everything inside the package. A package-m
anager install lands under `node_modules`, which may be pruned or relinked at any time, so user data
moves to `<DSH_HOME>/plugin-catalog` instead.
## Updating plugins
The updater changes exactly two things: the dependency spec in the profile's `package.json`, and wha
tever the package manager then does to `node_modules`. It never touches `dsh.profile.bundles`.
**It checks compatibility first.** Three failure modes are looked for, all of which have broken real
mpatibility first.** Three failure modes are looked for, all of which have broken real DSH profiles:
1. **A raised peer requirement.** The new version wants a newer peer than what is installed. (A real

incident: a session backend began requiring a newer DSH core than the machine was running.)
2. **A
reverse constraint.** Another installed plugin pins a range the new version would no longer satisfy,

so updating A would break B.
3. **A Node engine mismatch.**
Two details worth knowing:
- **Prerelease ranges are matched loosely.** Strict semver would reject an installed `0.1.5-rc.2` ag
ainst `^0.1.2-alpha.2` — a range DSH plugins actually declare and work fine with. Judging strictly w

ould flag nearly everything as incompatible.
- **A peer counts as satisfied if *any* reachable copy
satisfies it.** Core packages like `@deepseek-ai/dsh-credentials` exist twice — a possibly stale cop
y inside the profile and the one the running DSH install provides. The plugin asks Node the same que
stion the host asks (a resolver anchored at the DSH entry script) instead of picking a path by hand.
Verdicts are advisory, never silently blocking: an `incompatible` entry still has a **force update**
button, and every run leaves a rollback point.
> **A restart is required after updating.** The running DSH process keeps the modules it already loa
ded; new versions take effect on next start.
